673.title: Purim: turned upside down (Esther 9:1)
673.hook: on the very day meant for destruction, everything is reversed
673.tomorrow: Purim: two gifts to the poor
673.howItsDone: On Purim, the fourteenth of Adar (the fifteenth in walled cities like Jerusalem), Jews hear the book of Esther read aloud at night and in the morning, making noise at Haman's name, and many wear costumes and hold a festive meal.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Mordecai's warning, and the fast before Esther went in. Your line was before the feast, a fast. Did your one small fast get you ready for something? Tonight the fast breaks, and the feast is Purim. Day six hundred seventy-three.

Haman, the king's chief minister, wants every Jew in the empire dead. To choose the day, he casts lots, and the lot falls on the thirteenth of Adar, nearly a year away. That lot, in Hebrew pur, gives the holiday its name: Purim, lots. The book of Esther is full of plans that go exactly the wrong way for the person making them. Haman builds a tall gallows for Mordecai. Haman walks into the palace expecting honor and ends up leading Mordecai through the streets on the king's horse, shouting his praises. And by chapter nine, the book has a two-word Hebrew phrase for all of it.
screen: `PUR: A LOT CAST FOR A DAY.` → `A GALLOWS BUILT FOR MORDECAI.` → `HAMAN LEADS THE HORSE.`

segments.voice: Chapter nine opens on the thirteenth of Adar itself, the day Haman chose. The enemies of the Jews had hoped, the text says, to rule over them. And then: v'nahafoch hu. It was turned around. Upside down. Instead, the Jews ruled over those who hated them. The phrase is short, and in Hebrew it's almost a shrug: and it turned over. The verb is about turning something over. And it's the hinge of the whole book. Haman is hanged on the gallows he built. Mordecai wears the royal robes Haman wanted for himself. The day of destruction becomes a day of rescue, and the month of grief, the book says a few verses later, becomes a month of gladness. The Talmud adds a reversal of its own. In tractate Megillah, it says Haman was delighted when the lot fell in Adar, because Moses died in Adar. What he didn't know, the Talmud says, is that Moses was also born in Adar. Purim takes this idea and turns it into how the day feels. When Haman's name is read, synagogues fill with the noise of rattles and stamping feet. Some communities appoint a Purim rabbi who makes fun of the real one. The Talmud even says one should drink on Purim until one can't tell cursed is Haman from blessed is Mordecai, a line rabbis have debated ever since, and some read far more gently than it sounds. Purim is a holiday where the world, for a day, is allowed to stand on its head, because once, on a very bad day, it did.
screen: `THE DAY HAMAN CHOSE.` · `V'NAHAFOCH HU: IT TURNED OVER.` · `HANGED ON HIS OWN GALLOWS.` · `BORN AND DIED IN ADAR.` · then, large: `TURNED UPSIDE DOWN.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: find something that turned for the better. Settle, and breathe. Go back over the last few years, and find one moment that looked like a disaster when it happened: a rejection, a move, a door that closed, a plan that fell apart. Then trace what came after. What grew out of it that you wouldn't give back? You don't have to call it a miracle. Just notice the turn. Stay with it. The bell holds the time.
V'nahafoch hu. It was turned upside down: the hinge of the book of Esther, and the feeling of Purim. Today's word.
Your line: turned upside down. Today, when something goes wrong, say it once to yourself, and wait to see which way it turns. Day six hundred seventy-three.

674.title: Purim: two gifts to the poor
674.hook: give to at least two poor people; Maimonides says this outranks the feast
674.howItsDone: On Purim day, Jews give at least one gift of money or food to each of at least two poor people, often through a synagogue or charity fund so it arrives in time for the Purim meal, alongside sending food portions (mishloach manot) to friends.

segments.voice: Yesterday, v'nahafoch hu, the day of destruction turned over. Your line was turned upside down. Did you notice something turn for the better? Today, what Purim asks you to do with your hands. Day six hundred seventy-four.

If you've been near a Jewish community on Purim, you've probably seen the baskets. Neighbors trading plates of triangle cookies, wine, fruit, candy, sometimes with elaborate themes and matching costumes. Kids running them door to door. It's the most visible thing people do on Purim. But the book of Esther lists four things for the day, and the baskets are only one of them. Another is easy to miss, because it's done quietly and nobody puts it on a doorstep. And one of the greatest Jewish legal minds of all time said it's the one that matters most.
screen: `BASKETS ON EVERY DOORSTEP.` → `FOUR THINGS FOR THE DAY.` → `ONE THAT'S EASY TO MISS.`

segments.voice: In chapter nine, Mordecai writes to the Jews of every province. They're to keep these days as days of feasting and gladness, sending portions to one another, and, in the old Jewish translation, "gifts to the poor." In Hebrew, matanot la'evyonim. Evyon is a word for someone in real need, someone who has to ask. The Talmud reads the plurals closely. Gifts, at least two. To the poor, at least two people. So the minimum is one gift each to two people in need, enough to help them have a Purim meal. Then comes a rule that's almost the opposite of how giving usually works. On Purim, the codes say, you don't investigate. Whoever stretches out a hand, you give to. No checking whether they really need it. Then Maimonides. In his law code, after listing the Purim obligations, he says something striking: it's better to spend more on gifts to the poor than on your own feast, or on the baskets for your friends. There is no greater and more splendid joy, he writes, than gladdening the hearts of the poor, the orphans, the widows and the strangers. Someone who brings joy to these, he says, is like the divine presence, which the prophet Isaiah describes as reviving the spirit of the lowly. So the feast is real, and the baskets are real. But the gift that outranks them is the one that goes to someone who won't send anything back. Many people give on the morning of Purim itself, often through their synagogue or a local fund, so the money arrives in time for the meal.
screen: `GIFTS TO THE POOR.` · `TWO GIFTS, TWO PEOPLE.` · `WHOEVER STRETCHES OUT A HAND.` · `MAIMONIDES: THE GREATEST JOY.` · then, large: `TWO GIFTS TO THE POOR.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: give to two people. Before the bell, breathe, and think of two people, or two causes, who could use something today. Maybe a person you pass on the street. A food bank. A neighbor who's struggling. A colleague who's quietly overwhelmed. It doesn't have to be money; it can be a meal, an hour, a ride. Picture each one, and the moment your gift reaches them. Decide on both before the bell ends. The bell holds the time.
Matanot la'evyonim. Gifts to the poor: at least two, to at least two people, on Purim day. Today's word.
Your line: two gifts to the poor. Today, give your two gifts, without asking whether they deserve it. Day six hundred seventy-four.

675.title: Purim: masks
675.hook: costumes hint at hidden faces, as God is hidden in Esther
675.howItsDone: On Purim, many Jews, especially children, wear costumes to hear the Megillah and to the festive meal; the custom is described as part of the day's joy, and some teachers connect it to the hidden ways God works in the book of Esther.

segments.voice: Yesterday, matanot la'evyonim. Your line was two gifts to the poor. Did your two gifts reach two people? Today, the costumes, and what hides behind them. Day six hundred seventy-five.

Start with an absence. The book of Esther, a book of the Hebrew Bible, read aloud in synagogues every year, never mentions God. Not once. In the Hebrew text, there's no prayer, no prophet, no angel, no miracle that a camera could film. A queen, a minister, a king who can't sleep, a lucky coincidence, and then another. The Greek version of the book, made in ancient times, adds prayers. But in the Hebrew, the silence stays. And Purim's costumes, some teachers say, are a way of dressing up in that silence.
screen: `A BIBLE BOOK WITHOUT GOD'S NAME.` → `NO PRAYER, NO PROPHET, NO ANGEL.` → `DRESSING UP IN THE SILENCE.`

segments.voice: The Talmud plays with this. In tractate Chullin, the rabbis ask a riddle: where is Esther hinted at in the Torah? And they answer with a verse from Deuteronomy, where God says, in the old Jewish translation, "And I will surely hide My face in that day." In Hebrew, I will surely hide is haster astir. Hear the sound? Haster. Esther. The name of the book sounds like hiding. Esther herself is hidden, too. When she's taken to the palace, she doesn't tell anyone she's Jewish; Mordecai told her not to. The Talmud, in Megillah, even says she was called Esther because she concealed who she was. Her face is in the palace; her identity is under a mask. And the whole story runs on things that look like chance: a sleepless king who happens to have the royal chronicles read to him, and happens to hear about Mordecai saving his life. Jewish tradition reads those coincidences as God working behind the curtain. Not absent. Hidden. Wearing costumes on Purim is a much later custom, usually traced to Jews in Italy, where a rabbi allowed it as part of the day's joy. Explanations came afterward, and one that teachers give is this: on Purim, everyone looks like someone else, because in the story, nothing was quite what it seemed. The queen was hiding who she was. The coincidences were hiding a hand. A mask asks the same question every time someone opens the door: who's really under there?
screen: `HASTER ASTIR: I WILL HIDE.` · `ESTHER HIDES WHO SHE IS.` · `COINCIDENCES, OR A HAND?` · `COSTUMES: ITALY, LATE 1400S.` · then, large: `WHO'S UNDER THE MASK.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: notice what's under a mask. Breathe, and think of someone you saw this week who seemed fine. Cheerful at work, funny in the group chat, put together at pickup. Now imagine, gently, what might be under that: tiredness, worry, a loss they haven't mentioned. You don't need to guess right. Then turn it toward yourself. What's one thing you've been hiding behind the words, I'm fine? Just name it, quietly. The bell holds the time.
Purim. Lots, and a story where God's name is hidden and the costumes remind us to look underneath. Today's word.
Your line: who's under the mask. Today, ask one person how they're really doing, and wait long enough for the real answer. Day six hundred seventy-five.

676.title: Passover: clearing out
676.hook: the house is cleared of leaven; teachers call it clearing out puffed-up pride
676.tomorrow: Passover: a candle and a feather
676.howItsDone: In the weeks before Passover, observant Jews clean their homes, cars and workplaces of chametz, use separate Passover dishes, and formally sell or renounce any chametz they still own before the festival begins.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the masks of Purim, and a book where God is hidden. Your line was who's under the mask. Did you ask someone how they really are? Purim is a month before Passover, and the cleaning starts now. Day six hundred seventy-six.

In the weeks before Passover, observant Jewish homes go a little wild. Couch cushions come off. Car seats get vacuumed for cereal. Coat pockets are turned inside out for old cookies. The toaster gets put away, or given away. Kitchen cabinets are emptied and taped shut. Someone finds a pretzel behind the fridge from two Passovers ago. It looks like spring cleaning, and in a way it is. But the target is very specific. People aren't hunting for dust. They're hunting for one thing, and the Torah gives it a name.
screen: `CUSHIONS OFF, POCKETS OUT.` → `A PRETZEL BEHIND THE FRIDGE.` → `HUNTING FOR ONE THING.`

segments.voice: The word is chametz: leaven, or anything that has risen. In Jewish law, chametz is grain from five kinds, wheat, barley, spelt, rye and oats, that has mixed with water and been left long enough to ferment. Bread, pasta, cake, beer, cereal. The Torah is firm about it. In the old Jewish translation: "seven days shall ye eat unleavened bread; howbeit the first day ye shall put away leaven out of your houses." And not just don't eat it. Don't own it. Don't let it be seen in your home. That's why the cleaning goes into the pockets and the car. Why leaven? The plain answer is the story itself. Leaving Egypt, the Israelites had no time to let their dough rise, so they baked it flat. Matzah is the bread of hurry. But the rabbis heard something more in it. In the Talmud, tractate Berakhot, a rabbi named Alexandri prays that God knows what really stops us from doing God's will: the yeast in the dough. The rabbis used that image for the inner pull toward wrong. Later, Hasidic teachers made it personal. Chametz puffs up. It takes a little substance and fills it with air until it looks bigger than it is. That, they said, is pride. Matzah is just flour and water, flat, nothing added. Another teaching points out that in Hebrew, chametz and matzah are spelled with almost the same letters. The difference between them is one small stroke. So the cleaning of the house becomes a cleaning of the self: looking into the corners for anything that's swollen past its size.
screen: `CHAMETZ: GRAIN THAT HAS RISEN.` · `PUT AWAY LEAVEN FROM YOUR HOUSES.` · `THE YEAST IN THE DOUGH.` · `PUFFED UP, OR FLAT.` · then, large: `CLEAR OUT THE PUFFED-UP.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: clear one crumb-filled corner. If you can, go now to one small spot, a drawer, a bag, a car cup holder, and clear it out while you breathe. If you can't move, picture it. Then, as the bell holds, look inward the same way. Is there one place you've been puffed up lately: a story you've inflated, an opinion you've held too loudly, a credit you took that wasn't all yours? Just notice it. Let it shrink back to its real size. The bell holds the time.
Chametz. Leaven, grain that has risen: cleared out of the house before Passover, and for many teachers, a picture of pride. Today's word.
Your line: clear out the puffed-up. Today, when you catch yourself making something sound bigger than it is, say it again, smaller and true. Day six hundred seventy-six.

677.title: Passover: a candle and a feather
677.hook: the night before, a search for leaven by candlelight
677.howItsDone: On the night before Passover, families say a blessing and search the house for chametz by candlelight, often with a feather and wooden spoon and a few hidden pieces of bread, then recite the Aramaic nullification and burn the chametz the next morning.

segments.voice: Yesterday, chametz, the leaven cleared from the house. Your line was clear out the puffed-up. Did you say something smaller and truer? Today, the night of the final search. Day six hundred seventy-seven.

It's the night before Passover. The house has been cleaned for weeks. The kitchen is scrubbed; the counters are covered. And now the lights go off. A parent lights a single candle. A child holds a feather and a wooden spoon. Somebody else carries a paper bag. They walk slowly through the dark house, room by room, peering into corners, under the couch, along the windowsills. And here's the funny part: everyone knows what they'll find. Earlier, someone hid a few little pieces of bread around the house, wrapped so they won't leave crumbs. The search is real, and it's also a kind of game.
screen: `THE LIGHTS GO OFF.` → `A CANDLE, A FEATHER, A SPOON.` → `TEN HIDDEN PIECES.`

segments.voice: Bedikat chametz means the search for leaven. The Mishnah opens its tractate on Passover with it: on the night of the fourteenth of Nisan, one searches for chametz by the light of a lamp. Why at night, and why a candle? The Talmud says night is when people are home, and a small flame is better than daylight for this job, because you can carry it into holes and cracks where sunlight never reaches. A torch is too big and scary to bring close. So: one candle, close up. The Talmud also finds verses about searching with lamps. One is from Proverbs, in the old Jewish translation: "The spirit of man is the lamp of the LORD, searching all the inward parts." The rabbis set it beside the night search: a candle moving through the house, and the lamp the proverb says searches a person. The feather sweeps the crumbs into the spoon. The hidden pieces are a later custom, so the search never comes up empty, and so the blessing said before it isn't wasted. When it's done, the family says a short Aramaic declaration: any leaven I haven't seen or found is nullified, ownerless, like the dust of the earth. In the morning, what was collected is burned. Then comes the honest part of the ritual. You searched carefully. You'll still miss something. Jewish law expects that, and the declaration covers it. The search asks for real attention, and then forgives you for being human.
screen: `THE NIGHT OF THE FOURTEENTH.` · `A CANDLE GOES INTO THE CRACKS.` · `THE LAMP OF THE LORD SEARCHES.` · `WHAT YOU MISSED IS LIKE DUST.` · then, large: `SEARCH BY CANDLE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: look for one hidden thing. If you like, light a candle, or just dim the lights. Breathe slowly. Bring your attention close, like a small flame, to one corner of your life you don't usually look at: a habit, a resentment, an unanswered message. Don't fix it yet. Just see it clearly, the way a candle shows a crumb. Then let go of what you can't find tonight. The bell holds the time.
Bedikat chametz. The search for leaven, by candlelight, on the night before Passover. Today's word.
Your line: search by candle. Tonight, before bed, take one small light into one dark corner, of your home or your day, and look. Day six hundred seventy-seven.

678.title: Passover: the seder plate
678.hook: bitter herbs, charoset, shank bone, egg, greens and salt water each speak
678.howItsDone: At the Passover seder, a plate holds maror, chazeret, charoset, the zeroa, a roasted egg and karpas, with salt water beside it; during the Haggadah the leader points to them and explains, and some items are eaten at set points.

segments.voice: Yesterday, bedikat chametz, the night search. Your line was search by candle. Did you look into one dark corner? Now the house is ready, and the table is set. Day six hundred seventy-eight.

At the center of the seder table sits a plate that makes no sense as dinner. A roasted bone with almost no meat on it. A hard-boiled egg, often scorched. A pile of horseradish so sharp it makes grown adults cry. A sweet brown paste of apples and nuts. A sprig of parsley, or a slice of potato. And nearby, a bowl of salt water. Nobody eats most of it as a meal. It isn't there to feed you. It's there so that, at the right moment, someone can point at each thing and say what it means.
screen: `A BONE, AN EGG, A BITTER ROOT.` → `NOT A MEAL.` → `THINGS THAT TALK.`

segments.voice: Start with the bitter herbs, maror. Of the Passover lamb, the Torah says, in the old Jewish translation: "with bitter herbs they shall eat it." The bitterness is the taste of slavery: the Egyptians, the Haggadah says, made the Israelites' lives bitter. Some use horseradish; others use romaine lettuce, which turns bitter as it grows. A second bitter herb, chazeret, sits beside it for the sandwich later in the night. Next, charoset, the sweet paste. The Talmud says it recalls the mortar the slaves used for bricks. So the sweetest thing on the plate is a memory of forced labor. Then the shank bone, zeroa. It recalls the lamb offered on the night of the Exodus, and its name means arm, the outstretched arm the Torah says brought Israel out. It's not eaten. The Talmud even mentions using a beet instead, and some vegetarians still do. The roasted egg, beitzah, recalls the festival offering brought in Temple times. Some also see in it mourning, since eggs are eaten by mourners. Then karpas, a green vegetable, dipped in salt water early in the seder. The green is spring. The salt water, some say, is tears. Families arrange the plate in different ways, following different teachers. The mystic Isaac Luria laid it out in a pattern of two triangles, and families who follow him set it that way. Others simply line the items up. Under the differences sits one idea. The plate is a set of props for telling a story, so that the story isn't only heard. It's tasted.
screen: `MAROR: THE TASTE OF SLAVERY.` · `CHAROSET: SWEET MORTAR.` · `THE BONE AND THE EGG.` · `KARPAS AND TEARS.` · then, large: `EVERY ITEM SPEAKS.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: name one symbol's meaning. Look around wherever you are and find one object that carries a story for you: a ring, a mug, a photo, a scarf, a key. Hold it, or rest your eyes on it. Breathe. Ask it, quietly, what it remembers. Who gave it, or where it came from, or what it got you through. Say its meaning to yourself in one sentence, the way someone points to the bone on the plate and explains it. The bell holds the time.
Passover. The festival of leaving Egypt, and the seder plate, where bitter herbs, charoset, bone, egg, greens and salt water each tell part of it. Today's word.
Your line: every item speaks. Today, tell one person the story behind your object, or ask them about theirs. Day six hundred seventy-eight.

679.title: Passover: four children
679.hook: the wise, the wicked, the simple, and the one who doesn't know how to ask
679.tomorrow: Passover: it would have been enough
679.howItsDone: At the seder, after the Four Questions, the Haggadah's passage of the four children is read aloud, and many families discuss it, sometimes using illustrated Haggadot that picture the four children in very different ways.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the seder plate. Your line was every item speaks. Did you tell the story behind one object? Today, the people the story is told to. Day six hundred seventy-nine.

Any teacher, any parent, anyone who's ever explained something to a room knows this moment. You've told the story. Now the questions come. One person asks something sharp and detailed. One rolls their eyes and asks why anyone bothers. One just says, wait, what is this? And one says nothing at all, and you can't tell if they're lost or bored or shy. The Torah, it turns out, tells parents four separate times to explain the Exodus to a child. The rabbis noticed the four verses don't match. And from that, they built a whole page of the Haggadah.
screen: `ONE SHARP, ONE SCORNFUL.` → `ONE CONFUSED, ONE SILENT.` → `FOUR VERSES THAT DON'T MATCH.`

segments.voice: The Haggadah says: the Torah speaks of four children. One wise, one wicked, one simple, and one who doesn't know how to ask. Each gets a different answer. The wise child asks about all the testimonies, statutes and laws God commanded. So you teach them the laws of Passover, all the way to the last detail of the night. The wicked child asks, what is this service to you? To you, the Haggadah notices, not to him. He's stepped out of the circle. So the answer is blunt.
